prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Monthly mean ozone by monitoring station (language en).
Grid: 13 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Station" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 73px
  col 2: header "Jan" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
  col 3: header "Feb" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
  col 4: header "Mar" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
  col 5: header "Apr" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 6: header "May" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 7: header "Jun" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
  col 8: header "Jul" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 9: header "Aug" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 10: header "Sep" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 11: header "Oct" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 12: header "Nov" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
  col 13: header "Dec" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r0A: widths [94, 52, 52, 52, 53, 53, 52, 53, 53, 53, 53, 52, 52] · table 725×255px · row heights [36, 36, 36, 36, 36, 36, 36] · column headers wrapped 0/13 · tallest cell 1 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 365px
Design r0B: widths [73, 52, 52, 52, 53, 53, 52, 53, 53, 53, 53, 52, 52] · table 704×348px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 36, 60, 60, 36] · column headers wrapped 0/13 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 344px
Design r0C: widths [94, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 38] · table 551×580px · row heights [83, 83, 83, 83, 83, 83, 83] · column headers wrapped 12/13 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 136 · OVERFLOWS the box by 191px

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

log.raw: {"preferred":["r0A"],"acceptable":[],"bad":[{"design":"r0B","why":"The narrower Station column breaks every long station name mid-word (\"Riversi/de\", \"Northg/ate\", \"Westfi/eld\", \"Eastwo/od\"), making the row identifiers hard to scan; rows become uneven and taller, yet the table still overflows by 344px, so the 21px saving is not worth the legibility loss."},{"design":"r0C","why":"Squeezing the month columns to 38px wraps 12 of 13 headers and splits nearly every numeric value across lines, with 136 mid-word splits; the table becomes 580px tall and still overflows by 191px, so it fails both fit and readability."}],"contrast":null,"ranges":[[94,110],[52,56],[52,56],[52,56],[53,57],[53,57],[52,56],[53,57],[53,57],[53,57],[53,57],[52,56],[52,56]],"rationale":"At 360px the table cannot preserve intact station names, month headers, and one-line numeric values at the same time, so the best design accepts horizontal scrolling rather than corrupting the data. r0A keeps every station name and month label on one line, keeps all values on one line, and gives the twelve month columns near-equal widths because they play the same comparative role. r0B and r0C trade away the most important scanning cues—row identity and numeric integrity—while still overflowing the box. A phone reader must scroll, but with r0A the table remains internally consistent and trustworthy.","principles":{"general":["When a wide table cannot fit, preserve unbroken identifiers and one-line numeric values before minimizing horizontal overflow.","Columns that play the same role—here the twelve months—should stay close in width so readers compare them as a series rather than as unrelated fields.","Row headers are primary navigation; breaking them mid-word damages scanning far more than a wider table or horizontal scroll does.","Uneven row heights caused by wrapping in only some rows disrupt the row rhythm and make comparison slower."],"specific":["This is a 13-column monthly ozone table on a 360px phone viewport; twelve month columns plus a station label cannot be shown at once without either scrolling or destructive splitting.","The station names are long enough that a 73px content width is the practical minimum; anything narrower breaks them mid-word.","The month columns only need about 31–32px of text width, so 52–53px including padding is enough for intact headers and values.","r0A's 725px table overflows substantially, but the overflow is preferable to the 136 mid-word splits and 580px height of r0C."]},"tradeoffs":"A designer prioritizing minimal horizontal scrolling might be tempted by r0B because it saves about 21px, but it breaks station names and still overflows almost as far, so the tradeoff is poor. One could also argue for a fundamentally different mobile layout—transposing months to rows or using cards—but that is outside the column-width decision.","uncertain":"The exact upper bounds for the ranges are judgment calls: wider month columns remain readable but add scrolling, while the lower bounds are firm because below them headers or numbers wrap or split. Reasonable designers could disagree about whether a modest amount of wrapping in secondary labels is acceptable, but not about breaking station identifiers or every numeric value."}
